headline: Companies mandate AI use, tying it to performance reviews and career progression
summary: Amazon's Clarity system tracks developer AI tool usage, aiming for 80% weekly adoption, directly impacting performance reviews. Meta will integrate 'AI-driven impact' into all employee reviews by 2026.
details: Amazon's Clarity system monitors AI tool usage among developers, setting a target of 80% weekly adoption. This data directly influences performance reviews, promotion evaluations, and career trajectories within the company. Managers can track individual compliance with this benchmark.

The integration of AI proficiency into performance metrics means it is no longer optional for Amazon employees. The company's Forte review system now includes AI adoption as a required evaluation category, impacting raises and potential performance improvement plans. This reflects a broader corporate trend.

Meta has followed suit, declaring "AI-driven impact" a core expectation for all employees starting in 2026. Engineers, marketers, and product managers will all be evaluated on their effective use of AI to achieve results. This aligns with CEO Mark Zuckerberg's vision for an "AI-native" company.

Meta's biannual review platform, Checkpoint, now incorporates AI-driven impact into each cycle. The company also introduced "Level Up," a gamified program rewarding employees for AI tool experimentation, with progress tracked via dashboards. Training resources are provided for those struggling to adapt.

This shift marks an inflection point in 2025-2026, moving AI usage from encouraged to enforced across major corporations. The consequences for non-compliance are becoming more severe, making AI proficiency a critical factor for career progression in the modern workforce.

headline: SpongeBob speedrunners smudged Xbox optical disks with sweat and grease to exploit 'lag clip' trick
summary: This unconventional method allowed players to achieve record-breaking times in SpongeBob SquarePants: Battle for Bikini Bottom by enabling crucial level-skipping glitches.
details: Hardcore speedrunners of SpongeBob SquarePants: Battle for Bikini Bottom on the original Xbox discovered that strategically smudged optical discs were key to a major time-saving trick. This bizarre method involved applying sweat and grease to the discs.

The 'lag clip' technique, central to this exploit, involved rapidly pausing and unpausing the game. This action caused the console's laser to skip while seeking menu background music, opening up opportunities for level-skipping.

The competitive community engaged in extensive detective work, testing various Xbox console versions, optical drive manufacturers, and configurations. They sought the optimal setup to induce the lag clip consistently.

After hours of experimentation, speedrunners like SHiFT and Zim realized the condition of the disc itself was crucial. They found that a specific pattern of eight petal-like grease smears emanating from the disc's center was most effective.

This precise smudging allowed players to easily trigger the elusive lag clip without rendering the disc unreadable. The discovery was confirmed by other top speedrunners, including 'swagmasterdoritos', who admitted to similar unconventional disc cleaning methods.

While SHiFT's time of 40 minutes and 27 seconds remains a top record, the speedrunning community has since moved away from optical discs. Most top SpongeBob speedruns now play the game from the Xbox HDD, citing inconsistency and ethical concerns about potentially damaging game discs.
